I worked at a suicide prevention hotline. It wasn’t exactly what I pictured doing when I was a young lad, dreaming of a superhero-type career, and it certainly wasn’t the “romantic and fulfilling” life I’d imagine it being. But it was real and it was necessary. Each night, five days a week, I took calls. Strangers who hung up their lives on the line because they had nowhere else to go, or because the darkness had swallowed the light. People grappling with hopelessness, shame, and despair. I listened. I offered support. I linked them with professional resources. My job was to be a tether, a hand in the dark.

I didn’t talk much about my life before the hotline. My family didn’t approve of my decision to go to college. My parents had a pretty simple view of the world: Get married at the first opportunity. Get a steady job at a steady company. Have kids. Be happy. They had a vague notion that happiness was a pretty basic concept. I didn’t get married or have kids, but I did get a stable job at a stable company. I had a life. It was good, but not great. I had a boyfriend, an intelligent and kind young man named Daniel, who I was extremely happy with.

We’d been dating for about a year, and I thought that whenever I was asked about our future, it was safe to say that we were headed in the same direction. I was happy. Happier than I’d ever been, I might add.

I was in the middle of a conversation with a caller who had apparently called in to ask for help. Being a lich in the zombie apocalypse isn’t easy. Sure, the zombies generally ignore you. They’re not interested in anything as complicated as a human. That’s the problem. Getting humans to take you seriously. “Hey, want to go for a walk, buddy?” is a common reaction when asked to socialize. Most people assume you’re a very old, very creepy man. Which, admittedly, you are. Most zombies ignore you, too. What’s your secret? What’s your curse? All questions you’ve grown weary of answering. The only thing worse is when they ask if you’ve been bitten.

Life is generally comfortable, if lonely. You can do as you please with impunity. Resources are plentiful. The world is yours. All you want is some semblance of companionship. Which brings me to why I’m currently hiding in the basement of the local hardware store. The current occupants of the store are rather keen on zombies. And they’re no friends.

You don’t exactly get invited to the afterlife. Zilla usually found herself in the attic of the first house she’d zapped into undeadhood, which made her a sort of one-zombie-woman-slash-attic-rat. She was filthy, bedraggled, and her clothes were always too warm or too cold depending on how the sun shone. She was pretty sure she was dirty, but the sun always saw her as pristine. Her favorite game was to jump out from behind the drapes and scream “BOO!” at anyone who happened to wander in. Mostly she scared the cat.

One Saturday morning, she was having a particularly good time jumping out from behind the drapes and shouting “Boo!” when she heard a cough. Then another. Then a groan. Finally, she peered around the edge of the drapes and saw him.

He was sitting on the dusty rocking chair and coughing and groaning as if he had a terrible cough and the worst flu that ever was. His face was gray and there was a nasty oozing on his neck. His eyes were milky and bloodshot and he blinked slowly like a reptile. It was bad, no question. But that wasn’t even the worst of it.

“Hello,” she said.

He croaked.

This story takes place a year after the murders of my parents, and I am 25 years old.

My security system is second to none.

But you can hear people downstairs.

It’s a strange irony that a high-tech system can’t block out what is heard.

You can’t, for example, block out footsteps with a motion sensor. You can’t block out voices with the alarm. And you can’t block out the TV with any soundproofing that I can imagine.

My house has thick, soundproofed walls and windows. My security system is, as mentioned, top of the line. There are no holes for air to circulate so quickly. I have smart locks that will only open when I enter my passcode, which is a nonsense string. I have a home-wide intercom and video system, which allows me to see and talk to everyone in the house, no matter where they are.

It’s a lonely life, and it’s the only life I’ve known since my parents’ deaths. I know I should be out there in the world, but I’m not sure how to exist outside of this home, where I’m the only one who has a key. I have friends, but none of them have ever been here. And every night, when I lock myself in my room, I’m thinking about someone downstairs.

I’m not even sure that’s the right way to describe what I did in Aethelgard.

The game wasn’t a failure in the literal sense. The servers did, in fact, shut down after the company behind it found a better way to make money from us through the Cloud Server. Aethelgard never made a profit, but it was a success in a very abstract, theoretical sense. Aethelgard’s servers were online for three years, and it was the last online RPG game before Cloud Servers made the world of online games forget about traditional servers.

I’m not sure why I remember that. I’m not sure I remember much else. My life as an NPC in Aethelgard was nothing more than what you’d expect from an NPC. The idea was simple: In the aftermath of a kill, there was still information to be gained. It wasn’t so much a hole as a window. It looked like something of a large bird had nested up in the attic and, for its young, had created a burrow in the roof. The opening was about the size of a doorway. It sagged in the center like it was about to fall open. It was circular, like a face, the eye-socket on the left. Above it hung a frayed, blue cord like a useless noose.

I never understood why the Belvedere kept this hole. It was a bad sign in any hotel that its boiler malfunctioned at the same time as its air-conditioning. I had booked a weekend getaway at the Belvedere, and on Friday afternoon, the boiler blew in the middle of the lounge. The air-con then failed and we were all left to suffer in the oppressive summer heat. The night before, I’d been wandering the halls when I’d first seen the hole in the ceiling.

From the moment of my birth, the world saw me as an aberration. Most children were born with eyes as dull and ordinary as the dirt under their fingernails. Brown eyes controlled the earth. It wasn’t some lofty ideal; it was literally true. Farmers had brown eyes and good harvests. Miners had brown eyes and rich veins of ore. Judges had brown eyes and handed out fair sentences. They were practical eyes, capable of distinguishing between shades of brown as effectively as some could distinguish between breeds of cattle.

People with blue eyes controlled the water. It wasn’t their fault; it was in their blood. They could make fish swim faster, ice melt quicker, rain come sooner or later. They were skilled at sailing, able to feel the subtle shifts in currents and winds no one else could. Sea captains had blue eyes and crossed oceans on schedule. Doctors had blue eyes and healed the sick. They had the power of life and death in their palms.

People with white eyes controlled the sky. They could call down birds from the heavens, dispel clouds with a thought, conjure rain with a gesture. They were revered poets and painters, able to capture the fleeting beauty of a sunset or the ineffable spirit of a storm. They were the prophets and the philosophers.

Then there were the rest. Red eyes could control fire. Green eyes controlled plants. Purple eyes controlled magic. Orange eyes controlled animals. I could go on.

But I was the first to be born with yellow eyes.
